title: The Carefree Man Sleeps, While Sleep Eludes Me
intro: Al-Mufaddal chose this ode by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, an Iraqi poet who lost his sight in old age. From his sleepless bed the speaker looks out over the deserted homes of princes and over the misfortunes of his own people. Then his memories fill with bright wine, women’s voices and the pastures he used to ride out to at dawn. The last line asks what pleasure is left in remembering.

translation: The carefree man sleeps, while sleep eludes me.
Care keeps vigil beside my pillow.
1.sharh: Anxiety has a place at his bedside like someone sitting up through the night. The contrast with the sleeping man is there before we learn what keeps him awake.

translation: I have no bodily sickness, yet I am worn thin
by a care I feel has struck my heart.
2.sharh: Wasting away would ordinarily point to illness. He traces the physical exhaustion back to a grief that has found its mark.

translation: One blow that has befallen me, mark you,
is that the earth is barred to me on every side.
3.sharh: The map he knew by travelling has become a set of barriers. The startling address in mid-sentence is an old exclamation that calls attention to his plight.

translation: I cannot find my way even to a watercourse
between Iraq and the land of Murad.
4.sharh: A hillside watercourse should be a conspicuous feature to a traveller. He names the span of country once open to him so the listener can feel the size of the loss.

translation: Whatever you have told me, I know well
that my path is the path of the man on the bier.
5.sharh: Her reassurance cannot give him another destination. One old reading sees the wood of the bier, another an aged chief who had to be carried on a litter.

translation: Death and its many forms both stand
high in the passes, watching for my figure.
6.sharh: Death and the ways of dying take up watch on high ground. He can barely see his way across it, but they can make out his silhouette.

translation: They will accept no payment to redeem the pledge
short of my life, neither new wealth nor inherited goods.
7.sharh: The creditor has his life in pledge. The two kinds of property, acquired and inherited, exhaust what a man could offer in exchange.

translation: What can I hope after Muharriq’s people
left their homes, and after Iyad?
8.sharh: Two names open the view out from a single sickbed. If a royal house and a great tribe could lose their places in the world, his own decline follows a familiar course.

translation: The people of al-Khawarnaq, al-Sadir and Bariq,
and of the palace with battlements at Sindad.
9.sharh: These names are the surviving outline of a society. The battlements are still distinct enough to picture even as the people who ruled from the palace disappear.

translation: A land chosen for their father’s dwelling
by Ka'b ibn Mama and the son of Umm Du'ad.
10.sharh: The men who chose the site are remembered both for generosity and for poetry. Their choice makes the desolation more poignant than an anonymous ruin would be.

translation: Winds have swept over the sites of their homes,
as though they had all kept one appointment.
11.sharh: Wind has free passage where people used to live. Their common absence looks eerily deliberate, as though the whole settlement had agreed when to go.

translation: Yet there they once lived in the utmost comfort,
under a kingdom whose tent pegs held firm.
12.sharh: A kingdom stands like a tent with its pegs driven deep. The listener has just seen the wind blowing across the empty site.

translation: They settled at Anqura, where over their land flows
the Euphrates, bringing water down from the mountains.
13.sharh: The poet places Anqura beside the Euphrates. The river still carries mountain water past the place where Iyad once lived.

translation: Then comfort, and everything that draws us into pleasure,
comes one day to decay and an end.
14.sharh: The history of the settlements yields a judgement that can reach his own pleasures too. One day suffices to exhaust what once seemed inexhaustible.

translation: Had you looked to Gharf’s house for my consolation,
you would have found examples enough to count.
15.sharh: The examples now come from the poet’s tribal family. Consolation means being able to count how many people have borne a comparable loss.

translation: What hope after Zayd’s men, scattered over a girl,
killed or exiled after such goodly preparations?
16.sharh: A dispute over a marriage undoes a group well prepared to defend itself. In al-Asma'i’s account its people refused a match sought by the king, who drove them out.

translation: In their strength they chose the open country,
and their giver outdid all other givers.
17.sharh: They once chose exposed ground because they could hold it. Their open-handedness was as much a source of standing as their ability to protect themselves.

translation: If you see me worn out now, diminished
in what has been taken from my sight and limbs,
18.sharh: The wide view narrows suddenly to the body before his listener. The “if” holds the thought open until the younger man’s life comes into view.

translation: if I have disobeyed the companions of love and youth
and heeded my reprover, easy now to lead,
19.sharh: Love’s companions have lost their influence. The man who once ignored the reproving woman now answers to the lightest touch on the rein.

translation: I used to go of an evening to the merchants, hair combed,
free with my money, my neck supple.
20.sharh: The merchants deal in wine. He remembers how lightly both his neck and his purse moved when he dressed for an evening out.

translation: I have taken my pleasure, and youth has its delights,
in first-run wine mixed with morning rain.
21.sharh: The wine is the juice that runs first from the grapes. Morning rain is the water he remembers mixing into it, so that youth itself seems to have a taste.

translation: Wine from an earringed man, nasal-voiced and belted,
who brought it for the silver coins of homage.
22.sharh: Earrings, voice and belt bring the seller into focus. One old explanation identifies the coins by the royal image on them, to which obeisance was paid.

translation: A lad with two pearl drops hurries it round, sleeves tucked up,
his fingertips deep red from mulberries.
23.sharh: The eye moves from the merchant to the server. The red on the boy’s fingers is likened to the stain left by handling mulberries.

translation: Fair women walk like full moons and like statues,
and graceful women pass carrying great bowls.
24.sharh: Moonlight and carved figures supply colour and shape. The great serving bowls place the women in the same living scene as the wine and the lad.

translation: Fair women pierce hearts with a glance, their colour like
ostrich eggs in a scrape between a sandbank and hard ground.
25.sharh: Their glances are arrows. The second image asks the listener to supply the eggs inside the ostrich’s shallow nest and see their pale lustre.

translation: They speak kindly. Delicate women,
bright of face and tender of heart.
26.sharh: Kind speech supplies a quality the observer cannot see. The Arabic locates tenderness in the liver, a seat of feeling.

translation: They speak softly, confiding in whispers,
and get what they want without calling aloud.
27.sharh: The memory preserves the volume of the voices as precisely as the colour of the wine. The women can make themselves understood without drawing the whole company in.

translation: Often at dawn I made for distant pasture men warned against,
its channels dark green, a delight to pasture scouts.
28.sharh: The next pleasure of youth begins at dawn, well outside the settlement. Darkness in the watercourses means exceptionally rich growth to those scouting for grazing.

translation: Night clouds had poured rain on it. Its growth was thickened
by patches of safra and zubbad.
29.sharh: The dark green has a history in the rain of the night before. He distinguishes the thickening patches of individual plants the way someone familiar with grazing land would.

translation: In al-Jaww and al-Amarat, around Mughamir,
then Darij and the hunters’ thicket.
30.sharh: The place names trace a hunting ride across the upland. Their precision is especially affecting from the man who now cannot find a watercourse.

translation: I rode a long-legged horse, ready to break into a gallop,
a racer who holds wild game and rival horses fast.
31.sharh: Speed gives the horse the power of a fetter. An animal he chases is as good as tethered, and in a race he can catch the horses ahead of him.

translation: The lone bull, so sure of its speed, becomes our roast
as my horse shifts between a gallop and a measured run.
32.sharh: The solitary wild bull trusts its running power, yet the verse already sees it roasted. The horse overtakes it while moving between two paces.

translation: I have followed departing folk on a sturdy she-camel,
powerful, keeping clear of calves, dry of milk.
33.sharh: He changes mounts as the purpose of the ride changes. The she-camel can carry him after the migrating households without a calf drawing on her strength.

translation: A wild-ass-strong camel, spring grazing filled her hollows.
You cannot make out a tick’s resting place on her.
34.sharh: Spring pasture has left no hollows between her muscles. A tick looking for its usual sheltered fold gives the listener a measure of her condition.

translation: And now there is no savour in recalling all that.
Time follows what is good with ruin.
35.sharh: The wealth of remembered sensation ends on a word for lack of flavour or delight. Time has done to his pleasures what it did to the homes that stood beside the river.

1.1.2.head: الخَلِيّ
1.1.2.meaning: The person free of care, as opposed to someone kept awake by grief.

1.2.2.head: مُحتَضِر
1.2.2.meaning: Present at the bedside, with an echo of attending someone at the point of death.

2.1.6.head: شَفَّ
2.1.6.meaning: Wore me thin or wasted me away.

3.1.3-5.head: لا أَبا لَك
3.1.3-5.meaning: “May you have no father”, a conventional expression that can mark emphasis or dismay.

3.2.4.head: سَدّ
3.2.4.meaning: With barriers shutting off his route.

4.1.5.head: تَلعَة
4.1.5.meaning: A channel carrying runoff from a rise down to a valley.

4.2.5.head: مُراد
4.2.5.meaning: Murad, a southern Arabian tribe of Madhhij whose territory marks the far end of the range.

5.2.4-5.head: ذو الأَعواد
5.2.4-5.meaning: “The man of the wooden poles”, the dead man on a bier, or in another tradition an old chief carried on a litter.

6.1.3.head: حَتف
6.1.3.meaning: Deaths or the various ways a person may meet death.

6.2.1.head: أَوفى
6.2.1.meaning: Climbs to a height commanding a view.

6.2.2.head: مَخرِم
6.2.2.meaning: Passes or openings at the ends of mountain ridges.

6.2.4.head: سَواد
6.2.4.meaning: My figure seen as a dark outline in the distance.

7.1.4-5.head: وَفاء رَهينَة
7.1.4-5.meaning: “Payment for a pledge”, something offered to redeem what the creditor holds.

7.2.4.head: طارِف
7.2.4.meaning: Wealth acquired by its present owner.

7.2.5.head: تِلاد
7.2.5.meaning: Long-held wealth inherited from one’s family.

8.1.4-5.head: آل مُحَرِّق
8.1.4-5.meaning: Al Muharriq, a royal house of al-Hira, named by a traditional royal epithet.

8.2.4.head: إِياد
8.2.4.meaning: Iyad, an Arab people once settled in Iraq whose communities were dispersed.

9.1.2-3.head: الخَوَرنَق والسَّدير
9.1.2-3.meaning: Al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir, royal residences or sites associated with al-Hira.

9.1.4.head: بارِق
9.1.4.meaning: Bariq, a site among these Iraqi residences whose precise location is disputed.

9.2.3.head: شُرفَة
9.2.3.meaning: The projecting battlements at the top of a palace wall.

9.2.5.head: سِنداد
9.2.5.meaning: Sindad, a site or waterway below al-Hira associated with a palace.

10.2.1-3.head: كَعب بن مامَة
10.2.1-3.meaning: Ka'b ibn Mama of Iyad, remembered in proverbs for his generosity.

10.2.4-6.head: اِبن أُمّ دُؤاد
10.2.4-6.meaning: The son of Umm Du'ad, the poet Abu Du'ad of Iyad, famed for his descriptions of horses.

11.2.3-4.head: عَلى ميعاد
11.2.3-4.meaning: “By appointment”, as though all had fixed their departure in advance.

12.1.2.head: غَنِيَ
12.1.2.meaning: Dwelt or lived in a place.

12.2.4-5.head: ثابِت الأَوتاد
12.2.4-5.meaning: “Firm of tent peg”, securely established in power.

13.1.2.head: أَنقُرَة
13.1.2.meaning: Anqura, a settlement on the Euphrates in the Iyad tradition. Al-Qaysi also records the pronunciation Anqira.

13.2.2.head: الفُرات
13.2.2.meaning: The Euphrates, coming down from the northern mountains towards Iraq.

15.1.2-3.head: آل غَرف
15.1.2-3.meaning: The house of Gharf, a Tamimi line named for Malik al-Asghar ibn Hanzala, renowned for generosity.

15.1.7.head: الأُسى
15.1.7.meaning: Examples in which the sufferer finds consolation.

15.2.4.head: العُدّاد
15.2.4.meaning: Those who enumerate examples of loss.

16.1.3.head: زَيد
16.1.3.meaning: Zayd, ancestor of the group exiled in the marriage story.

16.2.5.head: تَآدٍ
16.2.5.meaning: Mutual support and readiness, a people well equipped to face trouble.

17.2.2.head: رافِد
17.2.2.meaning: A giver or supporter, matched here against the benefactors of other peoples.

18.1.5.head: غاضَ
18.1.5.meaning: Diminished me, as a body of water recedes.

19.1.3-4.head: الصَّبابَة والصِّبا
19.1.3-4.meaning: Love-longing and the impulses of youth, two words similar in sound.

19.2.4.head: قِياد
19.2.4.meaning: My leading rein, figuratively the ease with which I can be guided.

20.1.4.head: التِّجار
20.1.4.meaning: The merchants, here dealers in wine.

20.1.5.head: مُرَجَّل
20.1.5.meaning: With the hair carefully combed and dressed.

20.2.1.head: مَذِل
20.2.1.meaning: Free-spending, inclined to let money go.

20.2.4.head: جيد
20.2.4.meaning: My neck, expressed by a poetic plural, still supple with youth.

21.2.1.head: سُلافَة
21.2.1.meaning: Fine wine from the first juice to run from the grapes.

21.2.4.head: غادِيَة
21.2.4.meaning: Morning rain clouds, furnishing the water for the wine.

22.1.4.head: نَطَف
22.1.4.meaning: Earrings worn by the wine merchant.

22.1.5.head: أَغَنّ
22.1.5.meaning: Nasal or resonant in the voice.

22.1.6.head: مُنَطَّق
22.1.6.meaning: Belted or girded at the waist.

22.2.3-4.head: دَراهِم الإِسجاد
22.2.3-4.meaning: “Dirhams of homage”, explained as Persian coins bearing a royal image that received obeisance.

23.1.4.head: تومَة
23.1.4.meaning: Two pearl-like ear ornaments, possibly silver beads.

23.2.4.head: الفِرصاد
23.2.4.meaning: Red mulberries whose juice stains the fingers.

24.1.4.head: دُميَة
24.1.4.meaning: Like human figures carved or modelled with care.

24.2.3.head: رِفد
24.2.3.meaning: With large drinking bowls. Another reading understands the word through ardaf, hips.

25.2.1.head: أُدحِيّ
25.2.1.meaning: The shallow scrape where an ostrich lays, standing here for the eggs inside it.

25.2.3.head: صَريمَة
25.2.3.meaning: A distinct ridge or strip of sand.

25.2.4.head: جَماد
25.2.4.meaning: Hard, stony ground bordering the sand.

26.2.3-4.head: رَقيقَة الأَكباد
26.2.3-4.meaning: “Tender of liver”, gentle in disposition. Some commentators understand the physical flanks.

27.2.5.head: تَنادٍ
27.2.5.meaning: Calling out to one another across a distance.

28.1.4.head: مُتَناذَر
28.1.4.meaning: A place people warn one another against visiting.

28.2.1-2.head: أَحوى المَذانِب
28.2.1-2.meaning: “Dark in its runnels”, lush growth marking the water channels.

28.2.4.head: رائِد
28.2.4.meaning: Scouts sent ahead to look for grazing.

29.2.1.head: نُفَأ
29.2.1.meaning: Scattered patches or tufts of vegetation.

29.2.3-4.head: الصَّفراء والزُّبّاد
29.2.3-4.meaning: Safra and zubbad, two named plants in the pasture.

30.1.1-2.head: الجَوّ والأَمَرات
30.1.1-2.meaning: Al-Jaww and al-Amarat, two localities on the grazing and hunting route.

30.1.4.head: مُغامِر
30.1.4.meaning: Mughamir, a locality on the route. Other witnesses read Muramir.

30.2.1.head: ضارِج
30.2.1.meaning: Darij, a hunting locality also named by Imru' al-Qays.

30.2.2-3.head: قَصيمَة الطُّرّاد
30.2.2-3.meaning: Qasimat al-Turrad, the thicket or locality of the game chasers.

31.1.1.head: مُشَمِّر
31.1.1.meaning: A long-legged horse ready to run.

31.1.2.head: عَتِد
31.1.2.meaning: Ready at hand, in racing condition.

31.1.3-4.head: جَهيز الشَّدّ
31.1.3-4.meaning: Swift at full gallop. Al-Qaysi’s diwan reads jahir.

31.2.1-2.head: قَيد الأَوابِد
31.2.1-2.meaning: “A fetter for wild game”, a horse fast enough to arrest its quarry.

31.2.4.head: جَواد
31.2.4.meaning: Fleet and strong in the running, said of a horse.

32.1.1.head: شَوى
32.1.1.meaning: Makes roast meat of the quarry by running it down.

32.1.3.head: الوَحَد
32.1.3.meaning: A solitary wild bull or oryx.

32.1.5.head: حُضر
32.1.5.meaning: Its running speed, of which the quarry is confident.

32.2.1.head: شَريج
32.2.1.meaning: A blend of two paces, the gallop and a more restrained run.

33.1.4.head: جَسرَة
33.1.4.meaning: A sturdy she-camel capable of long travel.

33.2.1.head: أُجُد
33.2.1.meaning: Strongly built and firm of limb.

33.2.2-3.head: مُهاجِرَة السِّقاب
33.2.2-3.meaning: Separated from suckling calves, with no young drawing off her strength.

33.2.4.head: جَماد
33.2.4.meaning: A she-camel with little or no milk.

34.1.1.head: عَيرانَة
34.1.1.meaning: A she-camel tough as a desert wild ass.

34.1.4.head: خَصاص
34.1.4.meaning: The hollows in her frame that fattening has filled out.

34.2.4-5.head: مَقيل قُراد
34.2.4-5.meaning: “A tick’s midday resting place”, a sheltered crease in the skin.

35.1.4.head: مَهاه
35.1.4.meaning: Savour, delight or worth. Abu Ubayda explains the old word as what recollection has lost.

35.2.2.head: أَعقَبَ
35.2.2.meaning: Makes one condition follow and replace another.
